mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of "Wrongful Conviction with Maggie Freeling" tells the story of Laquanda Fay Jacobs, who was wrongfully convicted of murder at the age of 16 in 1993.  In 1992, Kevin Gaddy was murdered for his Chicago Bulls jacket, and despite having an alibi and not fitting the eyewitness descriptions of the shooter, Fay was arrested.  Key evidence against her was from eyewitnesses, one of whom repeatedly failed to identify her until pressured by police.  Her defense attorneys were ineffective, with one even presenting a conflict of interest and asking her to lie.  Fay was convicted and sentenced to life without parole, enduring years of incarceration.  While the Supreme Court's Miller v. Alabama decision offered a chance for resentencing, it came with a difficult choice: freedom with a felony conviction or continued fight for full exoneration.  Fay chose release in 2018 but continues to fight for a full pardon and advocates for others, highlighting the systemic issues of racial bias and ineffective counsel in wrongful convictions.

featuredIndividual.exonerationYear: Not exonerated, released in 2018 on time served, conviction stands.
featuredIndividual.sentence: Life without parole (original sentence), later resentenced to time served.
contributingFactorsRaw: Eyewitness Misidentification: Tony Davis's unreliable identification after initial failures and suggestiveness. Sean Riggins' recanted identification.
Ineffective Assistance of Counsel: First lawyer had conflict of interest and asked her to lie; second lawyer failed to investigate alibi, eyewitness descriptions, and present key evidence.

Racial Bias/Systemic Issues:  Mentioned as a potential factor, "racism, very simple," and racial profiling by police during initial arrest. Pressure to solve crimes due to gang violence in Little Rock.
featuredIndividual.status: Released on time served, conviction stands, seeking clemency/pardon.
organizationsInvolvedRaw: Midwest Innocence Project (MIP) - represented her in appeals and clemency petition.
innocenceLawyersRaw: Trisha Bushnell, Executive Director of the Midwest Innocence Project, is Faye's current attorney, advocating for her exoneration and clemency.
featuredIndividual.crossReference: Not explicitly stated if she appears in an exoneree database in the transcript.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: Kevin Gaddy and Tony Davis were robbed at gunpoint for Kevin's Chicago Bulls starter jacket. During a struggle, Kevin was shot and killed by a woman.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Eyewitness testimony of Tony Davis identifying Fay as the shooter.
Eyewitness testimony of Sean Riggins (later recanted) identifying Fay as the shooter.
No forensic evidence linking Fay to the crime.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes:
-   First lawyer, James Cluette, had a conflict of interest and asked Fay to lie.
-   Second lawyer, Bill MacArthur, failed to investigate alibi, eyewitness descriptions, file discovery motions, or present key evidence. Failed to highlight discrepancies between eyewitness description of shooter and Fay's appearance.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Four additional eyewitnesses who said the shooter was not Fay and were never called to testify at trial.
Discrepancies between eyewitness descriptions of the shooter (older, scars, different hair and clothing) and Fay's actual appearance (young teenager, no scars, different clothing).
Miller v. Alabama Supreme Court ruling on juvenile life sentences, which led to resentencing opportunity.

keyQuotesRaw: Maggie Freeling: "It's a literal Sophie's Choice Maggie, right? I mean, you have this intense pressure. You know that they have the ability to say, hey, we're going to leave you sitting in jail or prison for a year, two years or more while you await your retrial. Many, many strong, willed and brave and brilliant people have taken the plea because there's really no way out. And they just want to go home. They just want to get out." (Describing the pressure to take a plea deal)

Laquanda Fay Jacobs: "They knew all alone that I was innocent, but just wanted to use me as an example to other young juveniles. Therefore, I was railroaded into the system." (Fay's perspective on her conviction)

Laquanda Fay Jacobs: "I didn't comprehend that I was going to prison for the rest of my life. ...are you saying that I can never be with my parents again? I can never go back to my bed, you know, my home. So I'm losing all my friends. I mean, all this is going to be taking. Are you kidding me?" (Fay's reaction to the life sentence)

Trisha Bushnell: "You know, when you look at Faye's case and you look at the evidence, you can really just think, there's really no good evidence here, right? You can look at it and say, there's no good evidence. So how does she get convicted? Well, part of it is, it's just racism, very simple, right?" (Perspective on the lack of evidence and potential racial bias)
Laquanda Fay Jacobs: "You know, I'm just so happy to be free. Yet, I'm physically free, but I'm not free." (Reflecting on her current state - released but still a felon)
systemicIssuesRaw: Eyewitness Misidentification: The case highlights the unreliability of eyewitness testimony, especially when influenced by suggestive police procedures.
Ineffective Assistance of Counsel: Poor legal representation significantly contributed to Fay's wrongful conviction.
Racial Bias: Implicit and explicit biases in the justice system may have played a role in Fay's arrest and conviction.
Pressure to Solve Crimes: The context of rising gang violence in Little Rock may have pressured law enforcement to secure a conviction quickly, potentially overlooking evidence of innocence.
Plea Bargaining Dilemma: The "Sophie's Choice" of accepting a plea for freedom versus continuing to fight for exoneration, even when innocent.
Juvenile Justice System: The case highlights the harsh consequences of charging juveniles as adults and the life-altering impact of wrongful convictions on young people.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Call to action to sign a Change.org petition asking Governor Asa Hutchinson to pardon Faye Jacobs.
Implicit call to support innocence organizations to help individuals like Faye.
Implied need for reforms to address eyewitness misidentification, ensure effective legal counsel, and combat racial bias in the justice system.
personalNarrativeRaw: Fay describes the devastating emotional impact of wrongful conviction, including fear, isolation, and loss of her youth and dreams.
She highlights her resilience and ability to maintain her outgoing personality and help others even within prison.
Her relationship with Tiffany Woods shows the power of human connection and support during and after wrongful incarceration.

Her current challenges as a convicted felon, despite release and innocence claims, including difficulty with housing and adoption, underscore the long-term consequences of wrongful convictions even after release.
Final thoughts emphasize her feeling of being "physically free, but not free" due to the ongoing conviction and fight for exoneration.
